item.title: When Your Cofounder Is Also Your Spouse
item.description:
Career

When Your Cofounder Is Also Your Spouse

Two relationships, one nervous system—and what happens when only one gets energy.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Married cofounders transfer stress between work and home and between one another.
  • Emotional fusion looks like closeness, but the business creates false intimacy.
  • Working from home removes the last structural boundary between the two relationships.
  • The same neurobiological wiring that transmits strain can also transmit steadiness.
Source: Dall-E/OpenAI

They were six months into their startup when the arguments started bleeding. A tense product meeting on Tuesday showed up at dinner as biting remarks and avoided eye contact. A difficult conversation about household responsibilities on Sunday showed up Monday morning as reduced trust in each other's judgment. They couldn't quite tell anymore whether they were fighting as spouses or business partners. Increasingly, it didn't seem to matter.

This is the defining challenge for married cofounders I coach. It's not the workload, the equity split, or the market risk; it's that two high-stakes relationships now share the same nervous system.

Dr. Noam Wasserman's research found that teams with pre-existing social relationships are less stable than teams of strangers, with each additional social relationship in a founding team raising the likelihood of a cofounder departure by roughly 30 percent (Wasserman, 2013). For married couples, this compounds because the business and marriage become mutually dependent on each other's health. When one struggles, the other follows.

While that's not a reason to avoid building a company with your spouse, it indicates that the complexities of this relationship deserve extra time and attention.

Two Key Mechanisms

Psychologists use spillover to describe stress moving from one life domain into another. It's a mechanism well documented in work-family research (Edwards & Rothbard, 2000). Your afternoon shows up in your evening. Most people have a commute or a closed door in between. Married cofounders have nowhere to put it down. You can't decompress from your cofounder on the drive home, because your cofounder is home.

The second mechanism gets less attention and does more damage. Crossover is stress moving from one person to another (Westman, 2001). My strain becomes your strain. In most marriages, crossover has friction to work against—you don't know the people in your partner's meeting, and the specifics never reach you. Married cofounders have no friction. You were in the meeting. You already know what it means for the runway.

When the spillover and crossover effect co-occur, one hard Tuesday creates a massive ripple effect. It disrupts your evening, my evening, and our stress amplifies one another's, which then negatively impacts how we feel at home and how we feel at work. A vicious cycle.

Fusion, and What Stops Getting Fed

Identity fusion is the point where spouse, cofounder, and individual stop feeling like separate things. It sounds like closeness, but it usually means that none of those layers are getting the attention they need to thrive.

Running a business is absorbing. It gives you shared purpose, a sense of urgency and importance, and the feeling of being on the same side against the market. It can meet so many different emotional needs that the marriage loses touch with what it needs to thrive. You are together constantly and connecting rarely. Time goes disproportionately to the company, because the company is the layer with deadlines. The couple has none. It waits.

Intimacy is usually the first thing to thin. Desire needs some separateness to work with, and fused couples have very little left over (Perel, 2006). Then avoidance sets in. A disagreement at work is now threatening the stability in several aspects of your life, so you route around it. A grievance at home has a board meeting on the other side of it, so you avoid raising the issue.

Unfortunately, this leads to compounding emotional debt and resentment, which increases scorekeeping. Each of you start tracking your own contributions clearly and underestimating your partner's. Before long you're walking on eggshells at your kitchen table, managing tone, and avoiding eye contact.

Working from home removes the last structural boundary. No commute means no separation of space or moments of transition. The road map conversation and the marital conversation happen at the same table, in the same chairs, often in the same hour, which is a recipe for misunderstanding.

The Advantage Almost Nobody Uses Deliberately

The spillover and crossover mechanisms can accelerate positive outcomes as well. Research shows that when one partner is energized by their work, the other tends to be too, and the transfer is strongest when the receiving partner is paying attention to what the other one is experiencing (Bakker & Demerouti, 2009).

Married cofounders start with relational intelligence that founding teams spend years building: They have full context on each other, a long history of surviving hard things together, and no ambiguity about commitment. When the layers stay distinct, that becomes an operating advantage. The hard conversation happens in one afternoon instead of six weeks of carefully crafted Slack messages, because you've already had five hundred hard conversations and your relationship endured.

Your marriage is resilient, and you've built an ability to tolerate these cycles of rupture and repair in ways that most cofounder relationships haven't. However, this is only sustainable when the business and your marriage receive the energy they need to thrive.

Giving Each Layer Its Own Inputs

Rigid context-switching between marriage and business partnership is exhausting and often impossible. It's more important that each layer occasionally receives inputs unique to that relationship.

In practice, this can mean having date nights where neither of you talk about business, or strategic meetings where the sole focus is business and no personal dynamics are involved. Those types of separations can ensure that each facet of your relationship has the inputs and energy required to grow.

One strategy some teams have found helpful is naming the role you're speaking from. "I want to share some feedback with you, and it's strictly coming from an operational perspective. I hope you're open to hearing this as me wanting to continue investing in your professional growth." These small shifts in language can help maintain the integrity of the boundary between your personal and professional lives, and help give the listener adequate cues to receive information in clearer ways.

I also recommend naming the spillover out loud. "I'm still carrying that meeting" takes four seconds and prevents an hour of misread tone.

Many married cofounders find value in creating physical transitions. A walk, a change of room, a time after which company talk stops. Working from home, transitions have to be constructed, because they no longer happen on their own. Give the marriage a standing appointment the way the company has standing meetings, and defend it.

Because the demands of running a startup are all-consuming, the biggest danger is in allowing the business to be the primary source of connection at the expense of your marriage. Over time, this can lead to the marriage withering, which then contributes to operational issues and fallout across both domains.

What to Do Next

There's a piece of accounting I ask couples to do, and it takes about a minute. Look back over the past month and find what the marriage received that didn't arrive through the business; not shared time—the two of you were together constantly—but something that belonged only to the relationship. Most couples have to think for a while, and the thinking is the finding.

When nothing comes to mind or the results almost always include business, the marriage has been consumed by the company and needs fuel.

item.title: The Rewards of Parallel Careers
item.description:
Career

The Rewards of Parallel Careers

The benefits of devoting time, effort, and thought to multiple pursuits.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Parallel careers can be crucial despite today's precarious economy.
  • Parallel careers are prevalent in creative industries.
  • Keep your eyes open for limitations in time, resources, and potential conflicts of interest.
Source: Jozef Micic/Shutterstock

The beloved author Ann Patchett is getting rave reviews for her new novel, Whistler. Along with her writing career, she is the active owner of Parnassus Books, a bookstore in Nashville, and founder of a related nonprofit organization, the Parnassus Books Foundation.

That makes her an example of what the father of modern management advocates. In his prescient 1999 book Management Challenges for the 21st Century, Peter Drucker declared that “developing a parallel career” is an answer to the second half of one’s life. This is good advice for anyone, whether or not they are in or near that stage of life.

For many years, Drucker maintained parallel careers in writing, teaching, and consulting. When I interviewed him in 2002, three years before his death at 95, he said that “if you want to diagram my work, in the center is writing, then comes consulting, then comes teaching. I’ve never been primarily an academic. I like to teach because that’s the way I learn.”

Psychological and Financial Rewards

A parallel career can potentially provide both psychological and financial rewards for people who devote time, effort, and thought to working simultaneously on two (or more) jobs or activities. Thinking of your alternate pursuits as parallel careers can be more of a mental commitment than adding a part-time job, though technically it could fall into that category.

Knowledge workers are currently grappling with a precarious economy, particularly for employment. Professions (and academic fields of study) that once seemed solid and everlasting are now more tentative. Some people can’t find employment, or at least full employment, in their main field of endeavor. We must acknowledge that it can sometimes be difficult to have even one job, let alone two or more.

Yet since Drucker wrote those words 27 years ago, we have become more aware of terminology like the gig economy and side hustles. People want to express themselves in different ways, and doing only one professional activity can seem limiting.

Boards of Directors and Beyond

Many of Peter Drucker’s professional associates were adept at parallel careers. In 1990, Frances Hesselbein (1915-2022) and Bob Buford (1939-2018) were co-founders of the Peter F. Drucker Foundation for Nonprofit Management (now the Frances Hesselbein Leadership Forum), with Drucker as honorary chairman.

article continues after advertisement

While leading the organization, Hesselbein authored well-regarded leadership books, such as My Life in Leadership. She taught for two years after being appointed to the Class of 1951 Chair for the Study of Leadership at the United States Military Academy at West Point.

She also served on the boards of directors of both nonprofit organizations and corporations. She was the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Josephson Institute of Ethics, and a longtime board member of the Mutual of America Life Insurance Company. (The offices of the Drucker Foundation were located at Mutual of America’s headquarters building in New York.)

After a successful business career, Buford founded two personal growth-related nonprofits, the Halftime Institute and Leadership Network, while remaining active in the Drucker Foundation. He wrote bestselling books related to the work of his nonprofits, including Halftime: Moving from Success to Significance.

Leadership Opportunities

Parallel careers have become more common in recent years, especially in creative industries. Actors are often also directors, producers, teachers, musicians, voiceover artists, screenwriters, and playwrights. Many nonfiction authors in particular create their own businesses—they work as consultants, coaches, and teachers. Parallel careers can be seen in other fields as well, such as law and medicine; other professionals also teach, write, and perhaps devote time to areas such as music, painting. and sculpture. Many knowledge workers are involved in some form of retail activity, including entrepreneurship.

Engaging in different worlds helps you meet and interact with people you might not otherwise. The activities can lead to a heightened sense of self-worth and accomplishment. They can provide leadership opportunities that may not be on offer in your current work.

Eyes Wide Open

While there are undeniable benefits in parallel careers, it’s best to have your eyes wide open. These pursuits take time, planning, and effort. In some cases, they may be unpaid or low-paying. They may require additional learning on your part, or even new degrees or certifications. Consider whether or not parallel careers could dilute your strength by spreading your time and resources too thin.

You almost certainly have to make shifts in your life, especially in how you allocate your time. You can decide how well parallel pursuits fit your values. Do they compete or conflict with what you are already doing?

For some people engaging in parallel careers, it might not be accurate to say that one in particular is their primary activity, even if it is what mainly pays the bills. The main source of satisfaction could be one of the other areas, especially for people who pursue artistic and teaching endeavors as parallel careers.

article continues after advertisement

Conclusion: A Look Ahead

Taking on parallel careers can also be a way of previewing your life in the years ahead. Perhaps you will move more seriously into one or more of these pursuits, especially if you have to leave a job or plan to retire but still want to keep active. As artificial intelligence continues to gain momentum, Drucker's words can continue guiding knowledge workers in difficult times.

item.title: A Surprising Driver of Pro-Life Beliefs
item.description:
Sex

A Surprising Driver of Pro-Life Beliefs

Psychologists find that some opposition to abortion may be driven by mating strategies.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Prior research has suggested that opposition to abortion is primarily driven by religion and politics.
  • Recently, researchers posited that a deeper reason for pro-life beliefs may be a person's own sexual strategy.
  • A preprint study suggests that people more in favor of long-term relationships tend to be more anti-abortion.
  • The effect appears to be mediated by a belief in unwanted pregnancy as a deterrent for promiscuity.
Source: Joanna Malinowska / Freestocks

The issue of abortion is one of the most contentious in U.S. politics, split into camps that label themselves "pro-choice" vs. "pro-life." The Supreme Court’s 2022 decision that the U.S. Constitution does not confer a right to abortion has led to restrictions or total bans on abortion on nearly half of US states. It is clearly more important than ever that we attempt to understand why many adhere so strongly to a belief that abortion is wrong.

Elias Acevedo, a Ph.D. candidate in the laboratory of evolutionary scientist Martie Haselton at UCLA, recently posted to the preprint platform Research Square an article about how a person’s concerns over sexual promiscuity relate to their attitudes to abortion. (Preprints are articles that have yet to be accepted for publication in an academic journal or subjected to peer review, and so their results should not be considered conclusive.)

The psychology that underpins abortion attitudes is poorly understood, despite decades of research. The consensus is that the strongest predictors of opposition to abortion are religiosity and conservatism; people who are more religious and conservative tend to identify as pro-life.

Acevedo, building upon previous work by his colleagues in Haselton’s lab, notes that another, non-mutually exclusive explanation for pro-life attitudes is plausible. He refers to this explanation as the "strategic account," which is based on the following logic: People vary in their mating strategies, with some preferring long-term, committed romantic relationships and others preferring a larger number of short-term sexual partners. If a short-termer has a bad relationship, they can theoretically move on with relative ease.

But for long-termers, the collapse of a relationship can be more catastrophic. If a wife cheats on her husband and becomes pregnant, the husband may end up investing in children that are not his own; if a husband cheats on his wife, he may decide to leave her (and, potentially, their shared children) for his new partner, thereby cutting off investment in his first family. Long-termers may therefore be extra motivated to disapprove of casual sex, because it could be a trigger for the breakdown of their own relationships.

The important point here is that some long-termers may see abortion as a consequence of promiscuity. Acevedo points to Pew survey data suggesting that about 35 percent of American respondents believe that if legal abortions are easy to obtain then people will not be careful about sex and contraception, and the fact that pro-life arguments often frame an unwanted pregnancy as a consequence of casual sex. There appears to be a widespread belief that access to abortion limits a person’s fears about becoming pregnant after casual sex, an attitude that Acevedo and colleagues term "deterrence beliefs."

article continues after advertisement

The strategic account therefore hypotheses that people who prefer long-term committed relationships oppose abortion because they want to impose a penalty for promiscuity. This account does not mean that the standard explanation for opposition to abortion (religiosity and political attitudes) is incorrect, but rather that a deeper explanation is possible: “Religion and conservatism may… represent proximate pathways through which people’s strategic concerns about sexual behavior can be expressed as political and moral attitudes.”

Acevedo and his colleagues report the results of four similar studies, for which they analyzed data from a combined sample of over 3,500 U.S. adults. In all four studies, they found that persons who endorsed a more restricted, committed mating orientation (long-termers) tended to report greater opposition to abortion. As predicted, they also found that the link between mating orientation interacted with deterrence beliefs in predicting opposition to abortion—that is, persons with a more committed mating orientation more strongly opposed abortion if they also had a strong belief that pregnancy acted as a deterrent for casual sex. Religiosity and conservatism also partially mediated the link. The effects held regardless of whether data were collected before or after the 2022 Supreme Court decision to overrule Roe Vs. Wade.

The psychologists claim that their findings “indicate that views about fetal personhood or the sanctity of life are not the primary drivers of people’s attitudes [to abortion].” Their research also explains some unexpected behaviors and attitudes of pro-life advocates. For example, some (not all) pro-life advocates are willing to make exceptions for the victims of rape, while others support abstinence-only sex education even though comprehensive sex education has been shown to be more effective at limiting abortions. Neither of these positions make sense if pro-life advocates are primarily motivated to prevent abortions, but may be consistent with a strategic account of abortion opposition as primarily driven by a desire to deter casual sex.

article continues after advertisement

Acevedo and colleagues are quick to point out that the strategic account does not imply that opponents of abortion are disingenuous. Instead, concerns about casual sex may unconsciously lead to and be rationalized through religious beliefs.

Source: Joanna Malinowska / Freestocks

One possible implication of the results, if validated via peer review, is that efforts by pro-choice campaigners to persuade pro-lifers to their cause may be misguided if they are primarily based on proposals that seek to limit the number of abortions (e.g., making the case for comprehensive sex education). Acevedo and colleagues suggest another target of intervention: deterrence beliefs.

These beliefs are based on the assumption that abortions are usually the result of casual sex, when in reality nearly half of American women who seek abortion are married to or cohabiting with a partner; those who are not cohabiting with a partner are still likely to have been in a relationship for at least a year.

“To the extent that abortion opposition among sexually restricted individuals is contingent on deterrence beliefs,” observe the psychologists, “challenging these beliefs may offer a more promising avenue for attitude change than theological or biological arguments relating to the sanctity of life or fetal personhood. Understanding the motivational underpinnings of abortion attitudes may therefore help advocates, policymakers, and researchers better anticipate the conditions under which attitudes are likely to shift or ossify, and design more effective communication strategies accordingly.”

item.title: Beyond the Creator
item.description:
Spirituality

Beyond the Creator

Updating our beliefs isn't a betrayal of faith, but necessary evolution.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Psychological maturity requires us to dismantle the dichotomy between rigid dogmatism and absolute nihilism.
  • Healing requires building updated psychological support systems grounded in reality rather than denial.
  • Our task is to cultivate the capacity to logically modify our belief systems as new realities unfold.

This post is Part 2 of a series.

In my recent Psychology Today post, Why Humans Need a Creator: The Existential Imperative of Belief, I reframe faith as a cognitive shield for survival. Clinging to belief despite logic isn't irrationality—it’s an adaptive tool for psychological endurance.

But when the cognitive shields we construct to defend our beliefs sometimes shatter under the weight of an unyielding reality, the mind is forced out of comfortable rationalization and into stark confrontation. How do we navigate the psychological vertigo that occurs when sacred convictions dissolve into observed randomness? This article explores how updating our core beliefs isn't a betrayal of faith, but a necessary evolution to preserve our mental resilience and honor true logic.

When trauma breaks our belief in a structured world, it triggers deep disorientation, anxiety, and a sense of "meaning shock." To heal and rebuild, we have to establish new psychological support systems without falling back on denial or magical thinking.

This phenomenon lies at the heart of Ronnie Janoff-Bulman’s Shattered Assumptions Theory. Janoff-Bulman posits that we rely on fundamental assumptions—that the world is benevolent, predictable, and fair—as cognitive armor. When trauma shatters these baselines, psychological recovery depends on our ability to formulate a new, functional worldview that restores safety and meaning.

Constructive vs. Destructive Faith: How Meaning-Making Can Heal or Distort Us

The drive to believe can work for us or against us. There is a profound difference between adaptive faith—which cultivates resilience, agency, and growth after trauma—and maladaptive faith, which breeds toxic positivity, denial, and spiritual escape routes.

How do we know if our beliefs are actually helping us heal or keeping us stuck? We need practical criteria to evaluate whether our internal narrative serves our emotional well-being or masks our pain.

Clinical psychologist John Welwood famously coined the term “spiritual bypassing” to describe how people use spiritual ideas to sidestep unresolved emotional issues and psychological wounds. When we bypass, two main defenses take over:

Avoidance as Defense: Using platitudes like "everything happens for a reason" as a buffer to block raw grief, anger, or anxiety. It's emotional avoidance disguised as mourning.

Premature Transcendence: Trying to skip straight to peace or forgiveness before doing the heavy lifting of processing emotional pain, leading to a fragile, artificial serenity: “At least you have your health" or "others have it much harder."

article continues after advertisement

Hence, the antidote lies in integrative reframing: honoring the raw, unedited weight of grief—refusing the urge to bypass it—while gradually constructing a deeper, more honest framework of meaning, free from well-intended clichés that patronize instead of heal.

The Design of Purpose: Building What We Seek to Belong To

Recognizing faith as an adaptive "cognitive shield" explains why we cling to belief, but it immediately raises another crucial question: What now? If meaning-making is both a biological and psychological imperative, how do we transition from passive reliance on external order to active self-efficacy? The shift demands moving from passively seeking meaning to actively building it.

Psychologist Dr. Viktor Frankl famously identified the "will to meaning" as our primary drive, observing that the human mind cannot long endure an "existential vacuum." Just as the body suffocates without oxygen, the psyche fractures when stripped of purpose. Clinging to belief during tragedy is not mere irrationality; it is the mind exercising its ultimate freedom to choose meaning over despair.

These principles anchor Frankl’s work on "tragic optimism"—the capacity to maintain hope, find purpose, and remain resilient despite experiencing pain, loss, and suffering. Unlike "toxic positivity," which urges us to deny or gloss over painful feelings with forced cheerfulness, tragic optimism explicitly acknowledges that suffering and adversity are inevitable dimensions of the human experience, regardless of one's faith.

American existential psychiatrist Dr. Irvin Yalom built directly upon this foundation by framing existential groundlessness and freedom as therapeutic facts: when the universe fails to supply a master blueprint, the responsibility—and opportunity—to forge order falls entirely to us. In his profound work Staring at the Sun: Overcoming the Terror of Death, Yalom wrote: “No positive change can occur in your life as long as you cling to the thought that the reason for your not living well lies outside yourself.”

article continues after advertisement

Integrating this existential perspective with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) yields a practical psychological strategy. CBT is a clinically validated approach designed to help people recognize and transform maladaptive thoughts and behaviors. By illuminating how beliefs directly drive emotional states and choices, CBT delivers actionable tools to challenge cognitive distortions and establish healthier behaviors. For instance:

Overcoming Learned Helplessness: When traumatic events destabilize our baseline assumptions, helpless passivity deepens despair. CBT interrupts this cycle, teaching that agency is restored through small, targeted action steps rather than abstract rumination.

Behavioral Self-Efficacy: A meaningful life isn't reasoned into existence; it is built piece by piece. By aligning concrete habits with core personal values, we systematically re-establish the psychological framework needed for emotional strength.

Instead of waiting for external order or divine rescue to manifest, genuine self-efficacy requires us to become intentional architects—building the purpose, narrative, and structure we long to inhabit.

Flexible, Malleable, Logical

Clinging to divine discourse has long served as a vital mechanism of self-preservation. It aligns directly with an established psychological reality: human beings leverage agency and meaning-making to insulate the mind against despair and learned helplessness. However, these cognitive frameworks were never intended to remain static. To continue serving their protective function, our internal worldviews must be flexible, malleable, and grounded in logic.

True psychological maturity requires us to dismantle the false dichotomy between rigid dogmatism and absolute nihilism. This is not an "either/or" existential trap. We are not forced to choose between blindly adhering to archaic structures or collapsing into a void of meaninglessness. That would be missing the point completely.

article continues after advertisement

Instead, our task is to cultivate the capacity to logically and intentionally update our belief systems as new realities unfold. Just as our physical tools must evolve to meet novel environmental demands, our psychological contexts must adapt to foster genuine emotional endurance. Learning to refine and modernize our overarching narratives is more than an individual therapeutic milestone—it is a fundamental requirement for our collective survival and psychological evolution.

Lastly, if our search for a higher power is indeed an evolutionary apparatus for survival, then evolving what we believe is the ultimate sign of psychological maturity.
